precepts.text: Seest thou a man diligent in his business? He shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men. Business meaning God's business. This is why you see us meeting dignitaries across the world: because we've been diligent in God's business. Mean men are obscure men; stop wasting your time debating obscure people on the internet who only want clout.
precepts.point: The famine was over all the face of the earth, and all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn. That's what it's like when you have a plan, a solution. Joseph didn't sit around and wait for the dearth; the Most High showed him what was coming, and he made moves of preparation. This is how we have to be in IUIC.

note.label: Joseph in Egypt: Then & Now

precepts.why:
“at the end of two full years” Pharaoh dreamed of seven fat kine eaten up by seven lean kine, and seven good ears devoured by seven thin ears “blasted with the east wind.” None of the magicians could interpret it, until the chief butler remembered his faults and told Pharaoh of the young Hebrew. “Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh.”

Solomon wrote the precept: “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.” The business is God's business. Joseph was diligent in it in Potiphar's house and in the prison, and now a slave out of the dungeon stands before the king of Egypt. Even there he gave God the glory: “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace.”

And he did not come to Pharaoh with only a problem. He told him the dream is one, seven years of plenty and seven of famine, “because the thing is established by God,” and then he told him exactly what to do: appoint officers, take up the fifth part in the plenteous years, and lay up corn against the famine. To every problem, brothers, we must have a solution. Some spirits among us have a problem for every solution; stay away from brothers and sisters like that.

So Pharaoh said, “Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?” He put his ring upon Joseph's hand, arrayed him in fine linen, made him ride in the second chariot, “and they cried before him, Bow the knee.” We are going to tell the nations that too: bow the knee. “Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh”; he went in at 17 and spent 13 years in servitude and prison before he stood before the king.

This is why you see Israel today meeting dignitaries across the world: because we have been diligent in God's business. Mean men are obscure men, bums on the internet with a handful of followers who want to debate you for clout, whose numbers go up as soon as they see the shirt. They are not worth your time. A man diligent in God's business stands before kings.

precepts.text: Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord. That's the proof that the business is God's business.
precepts.point: The famine was over all the face of the earth, and all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn. That's what it's like when you have a plan, a solution. Joseph didn't sit around and wait for the dearth; the Most High showed him what was coming, and he made moves of preparation. This is how we have to be in IUIC.

note.label: Joseph in Egypt: Then & Now

precepts.why:
Proverbs says “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings,” and Paul shows which business that is: “Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord.” That is the proof. The business is God's business, serving the Lord, and you must not be slothful when it comes to it.

That is the business Joseph was about. He served faithfully in Potiphar's house and in the prison, he gave God the credit before Pharaoh, and he was fervent, not asleep, when the answer was needed. He is the diligent man who stood before kings.

So don't be over there asleep in the things of God. Be fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, and God will set you before kings and not before mean men, as he did Joseph.

precepts.text: Joseph foretold the seven years of plenty and seven of famine.
precepts.point: Joseph saved Israel in the famine and Joshua of Ephraim divided the land. Ephraim therefore felt more entitled than Judah, and the rivalry began long before the split.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
The division between Ephraim and Judah did not begin at the split of the kingdom; it was building long before. Part of it goes back to Joseph, the father of Ephraim.

Joseph was raised up to tell Pharaoh what was coming: “Behold, there come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt: And there shall arise after them seven years of famine; and all the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt; and the famine shall consume the land”, and “it shall be very grievous”. “And for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh twice; it is because the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass.” Joseph prophesied the famine and showed Egypt how to prepare for it, and by it Israel was saved when Jacob and his sons ran down to Egypt.

The same pattern ran through Abraham. After the Lord told him, “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house”, he came from Ur of the Chaldees beyond the Euphrates, up to Haran, and down into Canaan, the stretch called the Fertile Crescent. When famine struck Canaan, Abraham ran to Egypt too, just as Jacob and his house later did. The parallels line up.

So Joseph’s house carried a great deal: Joseph saved Israel in the famine, and later Joshua, of Ephraim, divided the land. That is part of why Ephraim felt more entitled than Judah, and why the rivalry that tore the kingdom in two was already there long before Rehoboam.

precepts.text: The vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another; the sevens in Pharaoh's dreams resembled seven years.
precepts.point: His spirit was troubled, and none of the magicians and wise men of Egypt could interpret the dreams unto Pharaoh.

note.label: Genesis 41: Pharaoh's Dreams and Joseph's Rise Over Egypt

precepts.why:
“The vision of dreams is the resemblance of one thing to another, even as the likeness of a face to a face.” Pharaoh saw seven well favoured kine eaten up by seven ill favoured and leanfleshed kine, and seven rank and good ears devoured by seven thin ears “blasted with the east wind.” The kine were not kine and the ears were not ears; the sevens resembled seven years.

It is the same way the butler and the baker each saw a variation of three, and the three stood for three days. Pharaoh saw different variations of the number seven, and the dream was the resemblance of one thing to another. His spirit was troubled, and none of the magicians or wise men of Egypt could read that resemblance and interpret the dreams unto him.

precepts.text: The Lord God revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.
precepts.point: The Most High reveals his secrets to his servants, and the secret of the Lord is with them that fear him. That is why the interpretation was with Joseph and not with the magicians of Egypt.

note.label: Genesis 41: Pharaoh's Dreams and Joseph's Rise Over Egypt

precepts.why:
“Surely the Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.” The Most High reveals his secrets to his servants. That is why the interpretation of Pharaoh’s dream was with Joseph and not with the magicians of Egypt.

Joseph knew where it came from. Pharaoh had heard say of him that he could understand a dream to interpret it, and Joseph gave all the praise to the Most High: “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace.” The secret was the Lord’s, revealed to his servant.

precepts.text: The secret of the Lord is with them that fear him; the Most High shows those things unto his servants.
precepts.point: The Most High reveals his secrets to his servants, and the secret of the Lord is with them that fear him. That is why the interpretation was with Joseph and not with the magicians of Egypt.

note.label: Genesis 41: Pharaoh's Dreams and Joseph's Rise Over Egypt

precepts.why:
“The secret of the Lord is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant.” The Most High shows those things unto his servants, them that fear him. Joseph feared God, and so the secret of Pharaoh’s dream was with him.

The magicians and wise men of Egypt did not fear the Lord, and there was none of them that could interpret it. Joseph could, and he said plainly why: “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace.”

precepts.text: A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself; that prudent spirit was on Joseph.
precepts.point: A prudent man foresees the evil coming and makes preparation so he is not consumed in it; the simple pass on and are punished. There is treasure and oil in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish man spends it up; spending irrationally is a spirit of folly.

note.label: Genesis 41: Pharaoh's Dreams and Joseph's Rise Over Egypt

precepts.why:
“A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.” That prudent spirit was on Joseph. He did not stop at the interpretation; he foresaw the seven years of famine and gave the counsel to prepare for them: let Pharaoh set a discreet and wise man over the land, appoint officers, “and take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt in the seven plenteous years”, and lay up corn in the cities, “that the land perish not through the famine.”

A prudent man foresees the evil coming and makes preparation so he is not consumed in it. The simple pass on and are punished. Joseph was wise, understanding and diligent, and that is what the counsel shows.

precepts.text: There is treasure to be desired in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish man spendeth it up.
precepts.point: A prudent man foresees the evil coming and makes preparation so he is not consumed in it; the simple pass on and are punished. There is treasure and oil in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish man spends it up; spending irrationally is a spirit of folly.

note.label: Genesis 41: Pharaoh's Dreams and Joseph's Rise Over Egypt

precepts.why:
“There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up.” Joseph’s counsel was the counsel of the wise: gather all the food of the good years, lay up corn under the hand of Pharaoh, and keep it in store against the seven years of famine. The treasure stays in the dwelling of the wise so Egypt could ration food through the famine.

A foolish man spends it up. Spending irrationally is a spirit of folly; had Egypt eaten through the plenty of the seven good years, it would have perished in the seven lean ones.

precepts.text: Children of Israel skilful in all wisdom and understanding science stood in the king's palace; the same spirit that was in Joseph.
precepts.point: The children of Israel brought to Babylon were skilful in all wisdom, cunning in knowledge, understanding science, and able to stand in the king's palace to give counsel; and they were taught the tongue of the Chaldeans, for we have the capability to understand multiple languages as well.

note.label: Genesis 41: Pharaoh's Dreams and Joseph's Rise Over Egypt

precepts.why:
The king of Babylon sent for “certain of the children of Israel, and of the king’s seed, and of the princes; Children in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science, and such as had ability in them to stand in the king’s palace, and whom they might teach the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans.”

That is the same spirit that was in Joseph. Pharaoh asked, “Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?” and told Joseph there was none so discreet and wise as he. Israel has always been a wise and understanding people: Joseph in Egypt, Daniel in ancient Babylon, and up until this day, a people responsible for many inventions and cunning arts.

The children of Israel in Babylon were skilful in all wisdom, understanding science, and able to stand in the king’s palace to give counsel, just as Joseph stood before Pharaoh. And they were taught the tongue of the Chaldeans, for we have the capability to understand multiple languages as well.

precepts.text: He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant; the king made him lord of his house, to bind his princes at his pleasure and teach his senators wisdom.
precepts.point: The Most High called for the famine and sent a man before them, even Joseph: sold for a servant, his feet hurt with fetters, laid in iron until the time that his word came; then the king loosed him and made him lord of his house, to bind his princes at his pleasure and teach his senators wisdom. Whether prince or common man, Joseph could bind any man in Egypt.

note.label: Genesis 41: Pharaoh's Dreams and Joseph's Rise Over Egypt

precepts.why:
“Moreover he called for a famine upon the land: he brake the whole staff of bread. He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant.” The famine was the Most High’s doing, and so was the man sent ahead of it. Joseph was sold for a servant, his feet “they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron: Until the time that his word came: the word of the Lord tried him.”

Then the turn: “The king sent and loosed him; even the ruler of the people, and let him go free. He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance: To bind his princes at his pleasure; and teach his senators wisdom.” That is Pharaoh setting Joseph over his house and over all the land of Egypt, with the ring, the fine linen, the gold chain and the second chariot, and “only in the throne will I be greater than thou.”

To bind his princes at his pleasure: whether prince or common man, Joseph could bind any man in Egypt. “without thee shall no man lift up his hand or foot in all the land of Egypt”; nothing moved unless Joseph decreed it.

precepts.text: Jacob refused to move his right hand from Ephraim's head, saying the younger brother shall be greater; he set Ephraim before Manasseh.
precepts.point: Jacob set that in place. When Joseph saw his father lay his right hand upon Ephraim's head it displeased him, and he tried to move it to Manasseh's head; but Jacob refused and said, his younger brother shall be greater than he; and he set Ephraim before Manasseh.

note.label: Genesis 41: Pharaoh's Dreams and Joseph's Rise Over Egypt

precepts.why:
Ephraim was the second born, but Jacob set him first. When Joseph saw his father lay his right hand upon Ephraim’s head, “it displeased him”, and he held up his father’s hand to move it to Manasseh’s head: “Not so, my father: for this is the firstborn; put thy right hand upon his head.” Jacob refused: “I know it, my son, I know it: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great: but truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.” And “he set Ephraim before Manasseh.”

That is why Ephraim, the one named for God making Joseph fruitful in the land of his affliction, possessed the kingship, and not Manasseh the firstborn. The first king of the Northern Kingdom, Jeroboam, was of the tribe of Ephraim, and Ephraim is the head tribe of the Northern Kingdom. Jacob set that in place with his right hand.

precepts.text: There came a dearth over all the land of Egypt and Chanaan, and our fathers found no sustenance; dearth is famine.
precepts.point: The dearth was in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread, because Joseph had stored up the seven years of plenty. All countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn.

note.label: Genesis 41: Pharaoh's Dreams and Joseph's Rise Over Egypt

precepts.why:
“Now there came a dearth over all the land of Egypt and Chanaan, and great affliction: and our fathers found no sustenance.” Another word for dearth is famine: no food, no sustenance to nourish the body. That is what the seven years of dearth were, “according as Joseph had said”, and it reached Chanaan where the fathers were, so that they found no sustenance.

But “in all the land of Egypt there was bread”, because Joseph had stored up the seven years of plenty. So Pharaoh sent all the Egyptians to Joseph, and all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn, for the famine was so sore in all lands.

precepts.text: He shaved himself and changed his raiment; Joseph had taken on the customs of Egypt as second in command.
precepts.point: This does not prove the Israelites looked like the Egyptians; the peoples were all dark people. The change was his age, his dress, and the customs of the land he ruled in.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
When Pharaoh sent for him, “they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh.” From that day Joseph was clothed in the customs of Egypt: shaved, in Egyptian raiment, decked out as the second in command.

That is why his brethren could not know him. The change was his age, his dress, and the customs of the land he ruled in. It does not prove the Israelites looked like the Egyptians; the peoples were all dark people. It was the shaving, the raiment and the years that hid him.
